stories.headline: The Satellite Internet War: Musk Vs Indian Regulators | Apple Smart Home & Xiaomi Air Purifier 6
stories.title: The Satellite Internet War: Musk Vs Indian Regulators | Apple Smart Home & Xiaomi Air Purifier 6
stories.summary: A high-stakes clash between global tech giants and national regulators has taken center stage over the future of satellite broadband in India. In this episode of Tech Today, Cyrus breaks down the regulatory standoff surrounding Starlink, takes a first look at Apple’s newly unveiled smart home hardware, and tests Xiaomi’s Mijia Smart Air Purifier 6 ahead of North India's winter pollution spike. The satellite internet debate escalated into a public spat after Elon Musk alleged that local business interests are obstructing Starlink’s rollout, prompting Indian authorities and Telecom Minister Jyotiraditya Scindia to firmly state that national security, data sovereignty, and regulatory frameworks apply equally to all operators. With India's satcom market projected to hit $14.8 billion by 2033, the struggle goes far beyond connecting remote regions; it is a battle over critical digital infrastructure, spectrum allocation, and stringent security mandates. We break down the government’s non-negotiable GMPCS requirements, including local gateway landing stations, strict real-time lawful interception, geographic beam kill-switches, and zero foreign data routing, alongside the economic challenge of high upfront dish costs versus low-cost Indian terrestrial 5G. In Tech & You, we look at Apple’s surprise smart home hardware announcements. Headlining the lineup is the Apple HomeView, a 7-inch wall- or table-mountable smart display priced at ₹39,900 that features Siri AI and recognizes up to six household members. Apple also introduced a refreshed Apple TV 4K at ₹39,900 with far-field voice microphones and Find My remote precision finding, the HomePod mini 2 at ₹18,900, and a broader connected home collection built with LG Electronics and Schneider Electric. We evaluate whether Apple's premium pricing can successfully challenge established ecosystems like Amazon Alexa and Google Home. Finally, as seasonal AQI levels begin to rise across Delhi-NCR and the northern plains, we test the Xiaomi Mijia Smart Air Purifier 6, retailing at ₹19,999. Featuring five-stage filtration with primary, HEPA, activated carbon, UVC, and negative ion systems, the purifier is rated for up to 940 square feet with a 443 m³/h particle CADR. In our real-world candle smoke stress test, the unit reduced an extreme 600 AQI down to 54 within 35 minutes and reached 12 in about an hour. We review its compact build, quiet 32dB sleep mode, app controls, and how it compares to alternatives like the Honeywell Air Touch P2. Should national security guardrails take priority over rapid satellite internet rollouts, or is the process moving too slowly? Will Apple's premium HomeView smart display find a place in Indian living rooms? Drop your thoughts in the comments below! Subscribe to Tech Today for weekly gadget reviews, deep-tech investigations, and digital policy analysis!

stories.headline: China imposes export controls on tunnel-boring machines sought by India, citing ‘national security’
stories.title: China imposes export controls on tunnel-boring machines sought by India, citing ‘national security’
stories.summary: The latest announcement comes days after Beijing announced a plan to impose export controls on 40 cutting-edge technologies, including those for advanced solar manufacturing and some AI platforms
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
event term: 'national security' in title weight 70
article_sentences: China on Monday said it would introduce export controls on tunnel-boring machines “to better safeguard national security and interests”, starting November 18.
India has already been facing difficulties in customs clearance and delays in importing TBMs from China for several critical infrastructure projects.

The latest announcement comes days after Beijing announced a plan to impose sweeping export controls on 40 cutting-edge technologies, including those for certain advanced solar manufacturing and some AI platforms.

The Chinese Commerce Ministry said on Monday in an announcement it was “introducing export controls on tunnel-boring machines and related items and optimising and adjusting export-control measures for certain dredgers and related items.” The measures will take effect on November 18.

The ministry said prior to the announcement, China had “notified the relevant countries and regions with which it has established export-control dialogue mechanisms.” “The items covered by these measures have clear dual-use (civilian and military) characteristics,” the announcement said.

“The measures are intended to better safeguard national security and interests, while also enabling China to better fulfil its international obligations, including those related to non-proliferation”.

India has previously raised with China the delays in customs clearance for imports of TBMs, which are used in India for several critical projects including the construction of metro rail networks in cities, railway corridors and key tunnelling projects, including in border areas.
India is dependent on imports for the machines.
Difficulties in imports from China started in 2024.

In October of that year, Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal had publicly raised the issue with visiting German Vice Chancellor Robert Habeck, pointing out that China was blocking the export of TBMs made by a German company in China.
On Monday, China also announced export control measures related to certain types of drones.

The controlled items include ”autopilots specially designed for Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs); UAVs or unmanned airships with a maximum endurance of three hours or more; certain engines specially designed for UAVs or unmanned airships; and UAVs with a range of 300 kilometers or more”, among other items.

stories.headline: Karnataka High Court Grants Bail To Pan Masala Manufacturer In Rs. 42 Crore Health Security & National Security Cess Evasion Case
stories.title: Karnataka High Court Grants Bail To Pan Masala Manufacturer In Rs. 42 Crore Health Security & National Security Cess Evasion Case
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
event term: 'national security' in title weight 70
article_sentences: The Karnataka High Court has recently granted bail to S. Nithyananda-the proprietor of M/s N Square Enterprises-who was arrested under the newly enacted Health Security and National Security Cess (HSNS) Act, 202 for allegedly evading cess amounting to around 42 crores.
The single judge bench of Justice S Vishwajith Shetty granted him bail on October 17[Saturday].

The accused had been in judicial custody since August 20, 2026, following a crackdown by the Directorate General of GST Intelligence (DGGI), Bengaluru Zonal Unit at his factory in Nelamangala, and his residence in Sheshadripuram.

According to DGGI, the search of the factory led to the recovery of six undeclared vertical Forms, Fill and Seal (FFS) pouch packing machines, alongside large quantities of raw materials, packaging materials, and finished pan masala goods.

The department had earlier alleged that the accused was engaged in unregulated manufacture and clearance of pan masala, without following the norms for registration, declaration of machinery, or payment of applicable cess.
After the search, the DGGI computed the alleged evasion around Rs 1 crore per machine every month, with a total liability of around 42 crores for the time period of February 2026 -August 2026.

After his arrest, Nityananda had filed bail applications which were previously rejected by the Special Court for Economic Offences on September 1, and thereafter, the Sessions Court on October 6, 2026.
Senior Advocate Sunil Kumar S., appearing for the petitioner, argued that the entire case rests on a presumptive calculation of cess.
He heavily relied on the recent judgment of the High Court of Karnataka in M/s Dhariwal Industries Pvt.
Union of India, wherein a Single Judge bench of Justice M Nagaprasanna struck down the capacity-based manner of levying cess under the HSNS Act as violative of Article 14.
Though the Division Bench then subsequently stayed the single bench order, the petitioner contended that the liability to the tune of 42 crores attributed is a disputed departmental calculation.
Kumar argued that it should not be treated as a final adjudicated liability at the bail stage.

stories.headline: Unleashing India's potential over 25 years
stories.title: Unleashing India's potential over 25 years
stories.summary: On October 7, 2001, Narendra Modi took oath as chief minister of Gujarat. Twenty-five years later, that milestone offers an opportunity to reflect not only on a quarter century of public service, but also on how profoundly India itself has changed during the same period.I have had the privilege of witnessing this transformation through the lens of business. The Mahindra Group has businesses across 20 industries that comprise nearly 70 percent of India’s GDP, including agriculture, mobility, technology, financial services, aerospace, logistics, real estate and hospitality. Across these sectors, one change has been unmistakable: The scale of the India opportunity has expanded dramatically.In 2001, India had enormous potential, but that potential was constrained by gaps in infrastructure, connectivity, technology and access. Today, India is a far more connected, capable and globally consequential economy.The numbers tell part of the story. India’s economy was around $500 billion in 2001; by 2026, it is close to $4 trillion. But GDP alone cannot capture the transformation. The more interesting story is how opportunity has increasingly moved from being concentrated in a few places and institutions to becoming accessible to millions more.Connectivity to opportunityConsider how an Indian citizen interacts with the economy today.A small entrepreneur can receive a payment instantly from a customer thousands of kilometres away. A farmer can access information through a mobile phone. A young person in a small town can build a business for a global market. A consumer can access financial services without necessarily stepping into a bank branch.Digital public infrastructure has changed the architecture of opportunity. Aadhaar, Jan Dhan and UPI have helped deepen financial inclusion and formalisation, while UPI has demonstrated how technology, scale and inclusion can work together.This is not simply a technology story. It is an India story: The movement from access being a privilege to access becoming increasingly ubiquitous.Also Read: 25 years of Prime Minister Narendra Modi in public office: Shaping governanceFrom infrastructure deficit to a new realityThe physical transformation has been equally significant.India has expanded its highways, airports, ports, metro systems, rail networks and digital connectivity at a scale that would have been difficult to imagine two decades ago. We are adding an airport a month for the past few years, and more than 30 to 34 km of roads daily, nearly three times the pace a decade ago. Electricity access, too, has expanded dramatically, with World Bank data showing 99.5 percent access in 2023.Infrastructure is not an end in itself. It is an enabler. Better connectivity allows a manufacturer to source more efficiently, a farmer to reach markets faster, a tourist to travel more easily and a young person to access opportunities beyond the geography in which they were born.What I saw from the industry sideMy year as President of FICCI gave me another perspective on this transformation.We worked with more than 500 CEOs and 30 ministries on more than 100 initiatives spanning Make in India, women-led development, farm prosperity and sustainability. I personally participated in more than 200 meetings with senior government leaders and saw first-hand how industry and government could engage on complex economic and policy questions.What stayed with me was the willingness to listen.Industry would bring specific recommendations, sometimes involving difficult policy choices. The response was often to engage with the substance: To ask questions,challenge assumptions and explore what could be done.Constructive dialogue matters. Government brings the policy framework and public-interest perspective; industry brings ground-level experience, investment and execution capability. When the two engage seriously, the potential for outcomes that benefit both the economy and businesses increases.I believe this partnership will be particularly important in India’s next phase of growth.Potential to executionPerhaps the most important change has been India’s growing confidence in executing at scale.Over the past decade, the country has undertaken large national programmes across financial inclusion, sanitation, housing, renewable energy, digital infrastructure and manufacturing. The pandemic provided a particularly powerful demonstration of India’s ability to coordinate institutions, technology, manufacturing and public systems at enormous scale.For business, this creates a new opportunity. India is no longer only a large market to serve. It can increasingly be a place from which to build products, technologies and businesses for the world.Manufacturing will be central to this next chapter.The global reconfiguration of supply chains presents India with an important opportunity. Initiatives such as the Production Linked Incentive (PLI) schemes have sought to attract investment, deepen domestic capabilities and integrate Indian manufacturers more closely with global value chains. As of December 2025, the schemes had attracted more than ₹2.16 lakh crore of investment and generated over ₹20 lakh crore in production and sales across 14 sectors.But opportunity is not automatic. Productivity, skills, logistics, ease of doing business and supply-chain competitiveness will determine how far India can go.At the Mahindra Group, we see this every day—in automobiles, tractors, electric mobility, aerospace and advanced technology. The aspiration should be straightforward: Make world-class products in India, innovate in India and compete with the world.The next frontier is peopleThe next 25 years will require a different kind of transformation.India’s greatest asset is its people. Our demographic dividend will become an economic dividend only if young Indians have the education, skills and opportunities required for the jobs of the future.We must focus on skilling youth for industry readiness with industry as an active participant.We must also unlock the enormous potential of women in the workforce. Greater participation is not only a question of equity; it is an economic imperative. A country of India’s scale cannot realise its full potential if a significant part of its talent remains under-utilised.Businesses, therefore, have a responsibility beyond creating jobs. We must build skills, encourage entrepreneurship and create pathways for more people to participate meaningfully in the formal economy.Growth must also become increasingly sustainable. Climate change, energy transition, resource security and urbanisation will shape the competitiveness of both nations and companies. Long-term value creation will need to consider financial performance alongside the impact on people, communities and the environment.From potential to prosperityPerhaps the greatest transformation is intangible.In 2001, India was often described through the lens of what it could become. Today, the conversation increasingly centres on what India can build, lead, and contribute to the world.Indian entrepreneurs are building global companies. Indian technology is reaching international markets. Indian manufacturing is becoming part of global supply chains. Indian innovations in digital payments, healthcare and space are attracting global attention.Yet confidence must be accompanied by humility. India still has significant challenges—from inequality and skills to urbanisation, agricultural productivity, and the creation of quality employment.Twenty-five years of public service, therefore, provides an opportunity not simply to look back, but to ask what comes next.The India of 2001 had aspiration. The India of 2026 has demonstrated growing capability. The India of 2047 must translate that capability into broad-based, sustainable and enduring prosperity.That is the next chapter of the India story and one that all of us have a role in writing.

opening: On October 7, 2001, Narendra Modi took oath as chief minister of Gujarat.
Twenty-five years later, that milestone offers an opportunity to reflect not only on a quarter century of public service, but also on how profoundly India itself has changed during the same period.
body: I have had the privilege of witnessing this transformation through the lens of business.

The Mahindra Group has businesses across 20 industries that comprise nearly 70 percent of India’s GDP, including agriculture, mobility, technology, financial services, aerospace, logistics, real estate and hospitality.
Across these sectors, one change has been unmistakable: The scale of the India opportunity has expanded dramatically.
In 2001, India had enormous potential, but that potential was constrained by gaps in infrastructure, connectivity, technology and access.
Today, India is a far more connected, capable and globally consequential economy.
The numbers tell part of the story.
India’s economy was around $500 billion in 2001; by 2026, it is close to $4 trillion.
But GDP alone cannot capture the transformation.
The more interesting story is how opportunity has increasingly moved from being concentrated in a few places and institutions to becoming accessible to millions more.
Connectivity to opportunityConsider how an Indian citizen interacts with the economy today.
A small entrepreneur can receive a payment instantly from a customer thousands of kilometres away.
A farmer can access information through a mobile phone.
A young person in a small town can build a business for a global market.
A consumer can access financial services without necessarily stepping into a bank branch.
Digital public infrastructure has changed the architecture of opportunity.
Aadhaar, Jan Dhan and UPI have helped deepen financial inclusion and formalisation, while UPI has demonstrated how technology, scale and inclusion can work together.
This is not simply a technology story.
It is an India story: The movement from access being a privilege to access becoming increasingly ubiquitous.
From infrastructure deficit to a new reality.
The physical transformation has been equally significant.
India has expanded its highways, airports, ports, metro systems, rail networks and digital connectivity at a scale that would have been difficult to imagine two decades ago.
We are adding an airport a month for the past few years, and more than 30 to 34 km of roads daily, nearly three times the pace a decade ago.
Electricity access, too, has expanded dramatically, with World Bank data showing 99.5 percent access in 2023.
Infrastructure is not an end in itself.
It is an enabler.

Better connectivity allows a manufacturer to source more efficiently, a farmer to reach markets faster, a tourist to travel more easily and a young person to access opportunities beyond the geography in which they were born.
What I saw from the industry sideMy year as President of FICCI gave me another perspective on this transformation.
We worked with more than 500 CEOs and 30 ministries on more than 100 initiatives spanning Make in India, women-led development, farm prosperity and sustainability.
I personally participated in more than 200 meetings with senior government leaders and saw first-hand how industry and government could engage on complex economic and policy questions.
What stayed with me was the willingness to listen.
Industry would bring specific recommendations, sometimes involving difficult policy choices.
The response was often to engage with the substance: To ask questions,challenge assumptions and explore what could be done.
Constructive dialogue matters.
Government brings the policy framework and public-interest perspective; industry brings ground-level experience, investment and execution capability.
When the two engage seriously, the potential for outcomes that benefit both the economy and businesses increases.
I believe this partnership will be particularly important in India’s next phase of growth.
Potential to executionPerhaps the most important change has been India’s growing confidence in executing at scale.
Over the past decade, the country has undertaken large national programmes across financial inclusion, sanitation, housing, renewable energy, digital infrastructure and manufacturing.
The pandemic provided a particularly powerful demonstration of India’s ability to coordinate institutions, technology, manufacturing and public systems at enormous scale.
For business, this creates a new opportunity.
India is no longer only a large market to serve.
It can increasingly be a place from which to build products, technologies and businesses for the world.
Manufacturing will be central to this next chapter.
The global reconfiguration of supply chains presents India with an important opportunity.

Initiatives such as the Production Linked Incentive (PLI) schemes have sought to attract investment, deepen domestic capabilities and integrate Indian manufacturers more closely with global value chains.
As of December 2025, the schemes had attracted more than ₹2.16 lakh crore of investment and generated over ₹20 lakh crore in production and sales across 14 sectors.
But opportunity is not automatic.
Productivity, skills, logistics, ease of doing business and supply-chain competitiveness will determine how far India can go.
At the Mahindra Group, we see this every day—in automobiles, tractors, electric mobility, aerospace and advanced technology.
The aspiration should be straightforward: Make world-class products in India, innovate in India and compete with the world.
The next frontier is people.
The next 25 years will require a different kind of transformation.
India’s greatest asset is its people.
Our demographic dividend will become an economic dividend only if young Indians have the education, skills and opportunities required for the jobs of the future.
We must focus on skilling youth for industry readiness with industry as an active participant.
We must also unlock the enormous potential of women in the workforce.
Greater participation is not only a question of equity; it is an economic imperative.
A country of India’s scale cannot realise its full potential if a significant part of its talent remains under-utilised.
Businesses, therefore, have a responsibility beyond creating jobs.
We must build skills, encourage entrepreneurship and create pathways for more people to participate meaningfully in the formal economy.
Growth must also become increasingly sustainable.
Climate change, energy transition, resource security and urbanisation will shape the competitiveness of both nations and companies.
Long-term value creation will need to consider financial performance alongside the impact on people, communities and the environment.
From potential to prosperityPerhaps the greatest transformation is intangible.
In 2001, India was often described through the lens of what it could become.
Today, the conversation increasingly centres on what India can build, lead, and contribute to the world.
Indian entrepreneurs are building global companies.
Indian technology is reaching international markets.
Indian manufacturing is becoming part of global supply chains.
Indian innovations in digital payments, healthcare and space are attracting global attention.
Yet confidence must be accompanied by humility.
India still has significant challenges—from inequality and skills to urbanisation, agricultural productivity, and the creation of quality employment.
Twenty-five years of public service, therefore, provides an opportunity not simply to look back, but to ask what comes next.
The India of 2001 had aspiration.
The India of 2026 has demonstrated growing capability.
The India of 2047 must translate that capability into broad-based, sustainable and enduring prosperity.
That is the next chapter of the India story and one that all of us have a role in writing.

stories.headline: 25 years of Prime Minister Narendra Modi in public office: Shaping governance
stories.title: 25 years of Prime Minister Narendra Modi in public office: Shaping governance
stories.summary: Any person, place, organisation or nation would change with time. If the period is 25 years, these changes can be expected to be deeper, wider, profound and fundamental.None of this commonsense anticipation could have prepared India and the world for the distance the country has traversed since Narendra Modi assumed public office for the first time—on October 7, 2001—as Gujarat’s chief minister. To put these momentous changes in perspective and construe what they augur for the future, we sought out some of the best and brightest minds, a select group that has been in the thick of things one way or the other.What emerges is that India has indeed transformed its economy, infrastructure, digital architecture, foreign policy, workforce, tax laws, energy mix, space programme, treatment of companies, approach to investors, and many other areas that influence the economy and industry, as well as human life in general. But there is another change—more subtle but just as impactful, perhaps more. Which is the way Indians, filled with never-seen-before self-assurance and ambition, view themselves and their place in the world.Anish Shah, group CEO of Mahindra Group, says in his article that the numbers tell only part of the story. Sure, it is nothing short of stupendous that India’s economy has grown from $500 billion in 2001 to nearly $4 trillion. But the more interesting story is “how opportunity has increasingly moved from being concentrated in a few places and institutions to becoming accessible to millions more”.Also Read: Unleashing India's potential over 25 yearsAshishkumar Chauhan, writing for us while still emerging from the demanding process of orchestrating one of the largest IPOs in India’s capital markets history, points out that when Modi took charge as Gujarat’s chief minister for the first time, the state was still reeling from the Kutch earthquake of January that year. “He did not inherit a growth story; he had to build one,” says the CEO of the National Stock Exchange of India.What a story it turned out to be! That combination of infrastructure first, direct investor engagement and follow-through became the template later scaled nationally. Modi’s stated philosophy, Chauhan says, is together with all, development for all, trust of all, and effort of all. “In capital markets, at least,” he says, “that has taken a concrete form: The growth of Indian enterprise is increasingly being funded by Indian savers.”Arundhati Bhattacharya, CEO of Salesforce South Asia, sees it as the story of how a country once defined by scarcity, distance and administrative complexity began using technology to turn scale into economic strength. The figures, she says, illustrate a distinctive Indian model. “The government helped build common rails and establish trust; banks, fintechs, businesses and millions of citizens converted them into everyday utility. The result has been a large, low-cost arena for innovation,” says Bhattacharya.Pawan Chandana, whose startup Skyroot is soaring on the fuel of the government’s space policies, says the biggest transformation is harder to quantify and describes it as “the expansion of what young Indians believe they can build”.Kiran Mazumdar-Shaw, Biocon’s executive chairperson, shares this belief. “The most consequential change,” she says, “has been the emergence of self-belief.”Sunil Kant Munjal, chairman of The Hero Enterprise, describes it as the “permission to think big”. opening: Any person, place, organisation or nation would change with time.
If the period is 25 years, these changes can be expected to be deeper, wider, profound and fundamental.
body: None of this commonsense anticipation could have prepared India and the world for the distance the country has traversed since Narendra Modi assumed public office for the first time—on October 7, 2001—as Gujarat’s chief minister.

To put these momentous changes in perspective and construe what they augur for the future, we sought out some of the best and brightest minds, a select group that has been in the thick of things one way or the other.

What emerges is that India has indeed transformed its economy, infrastructure, digital architecture, foreign policy, workforce, tax laws, energy mix, space programme, treatment of companies, approach to investors, and many other areas that influence the economy and industry, as well as human life in general.
But there is another change—more subtle but just as impactful, perhaps more.
Which is the way Indians, filled with never-seen-before self-assurance and ambition, view themselves and their place in the world.
Anish Shah, group CEO of Mahindra Group, says in his article that the numbers tell only part of the story.
Sure, it is nothing short of stupendous that India’s economy has grown from $500 billion in 2001 to nearly $4 trillion.
But the more interesting story is “how opportunity has increasingly moved from being concentrated in a few places and institutions to becoming accessible to millions more”.

Ashishkumar Chauhan, writing for us while still emerging from the demanding process of orchestrating one of the largest IPOs in India’s capital markets history, points out that when Modi took charge as Gujarat’s chief minister for the first time, the state was still reeling from the Kutch earthquake of January that year.
“He did not inherit a growth story; he had to build one,” says the CEO of the National Stock Exchange of India.
What a story it turned out to be!
That combination of infrastructure first, direct investor engagement and follow-through became the template later scaled nationally.
Modi’s stated philosophy, Chauhan says, is together with all, development for all, trust of all, and effort of all.

“In capital markets, at least,” he says, “that has taken a concrete form: The growth of Indian enterprise is increasingly being funded by Indian savers.” Arundhati Bhattacharya, CEO of Salesforce South Asia, sees it as the story of how a country once defined by scarcity, distance and administrative complexity began using technology to turn scale into economic strength.
The figures, she says, illustrate a distinctive Indian model.
“The government helped build common rails and establish trust; banks, fintechs, businesses and millions of citizens converted them into everyday utility.
The result has been a large, low-cost arena for innovation,” says Bhattacharya.

Pawan Chandana, whose startup Skyroot is soaring on the fuel of the government’s space policies, says the biggest transformation is harder to quantify and describes it as “the expansion of what young Indians believe they can build”.
Kiran Mazumdar-Shaw, Biocon’s executive chairperson, shares this belief.
“The most consequential change,” she says, “has been the emergence of self-belief.” Sunil Kant Munjal, chairman of The Hero Enterprise, describes it as the “permission to think big”.
The biggest change of the last quarter century, he says, is not a single policy but the mindset change.
“India gave itself permission to think big without losing track of the granular.
A significant part of that shift traces back to the man who took charge in Gandhinagar that October, and who has now spent a quarter-century in government,” says Munjal.
Pratyush Kumar, Sarvam AI’s co-founder, points out that in 2001, the idea that India could build digital infrastructure for a billion people would have sounded like a distant aspiration.
Few countries had attempted anything like it.
“What emerged over the next two decades was an unusual consequence, with the state building the foundation on which private enterprise could build at scale,” he says.

Sumant Sinha, who calls his renewable energy firm ReNew “a product of Prime Minister Modi’s larger vision”, says the sense of certainty and pursuit of execution that Modi has brought have changed the feel of India.
The biggest change, for him, is not any individual programme but that prosperity feels more widely distributed.
“Above all, one senses that millions more Indians now expect their children to live better lives than they did,” says Sinha.
Of course, the job is far from done.
Suman Bery, economist and former vice chairman of Niti Aayog, the government’s think tank, says: “It would be fatal to assume that, despite the past record, a steady 6 percent growth is assured.

It is not, and we are where we are only because our style of governance has proven to be flexible.” In his view, policy focus should be less on sectors and more on factors of production: Labour, land and capital.
Shah of Mahindra says the India of 2001 had aspiration and the India of 2026 has demonstrated growing capability.

“The India of 2047,” he says, “must translate that capability into broad-based, sustainable and enduring prosperity.” Bhattacharya of Salesforce says the next wave—powered by artificial intelligence, trusted data and automation—could make Indian businesses more productive and globally competitive.
“But durable value will require organisations to redesign work, develop skills and retain human judgement.”

stories.summary: Operationalizing on the auspicious day of Maha Navami, the historic India - New Zealand Free Trade Agreement unlocks unprecedented trade avenues, announced Commerce and Industry Minister Piyush Goyal! Indian exporters, MSMEs, artisans, and women entrepreneurs secure 100% duty-free access across New Zealand’s markets, opening massive export routes for textiles, leather, footwear, coffee, spices, and advanced engineering goods. The deal balances aggressive growth with vital domestic safeguards, fully protecting sensitive agricultural commodities like dairy, onions, chana, and sugar from zero-tariff competition. A dedicated agricultural productivity partnership will establish centers of excellence for kiwifruit, apples, and honey to raise farm incomes. Off the field, the two nations celebrate a century of sporting ties with the Black Caps debuting a special Maori-Indian jersey. Watch the complete breakdown.

stories.headline: Supreme Court stays execution of death sentence of convict in 2008 Ahmedabad serial blasts case
stories.title: Supreme Court stays execution of death sentence of convict in 2008 Ahmedabad serial blasts case
stories.summary: On July 7, the high court upheld the death sentences of 38 operatives of terror outfit Indian Mujahideen in the serial-bomb-blasts case
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
event term: 'supreme court' in title weight 44
article_sentences: The Supreme Court has stayed the execution of the death sentence handed down to an Indian Mujahideen operative for his role in the 2008 Ahmedabad serial bomb blasts that left 56 people dead.
A bench of Justices Vikram Nath, Sandeep Mehta and Aparesh Kumar Singh agreed to hear a plea filed by convict Mohammad Tanvir, who has challenged the Gujarat High Court's July 7 verdict.
On July 7, the high court upheld the death sentences of 38 operatives of terror outfit Indian Mujahideen in the serial-bomb-blasts case.
The High Court had cited the large number of casualties, the "humongous" nature of the conspiracy and the intention to spread widespread terror as key reasons for affirming the punishment.
On July 26, 2008, a series of 21 bomb blasts ripped through different areas of Ahmedabad in a span of 70 minutes, killing 56 people and leaving more than 200 injured.
"There shall be stay of execution of the death sentence awarded to the appellant (Tanvir)," the top court said in its October 9 order.
It said the original records of the case be summoned from the Trial Court and the High Court.
The apex court asked the Gujarat government to place the reports of all probation officers relating to the appellant before it within eight weeks.

It directed the superintendent of the jail concerned to submit a report with regard to the nature of work that has been performed by the appellant while in prison and also regarding his conduct and behaviour within eight weeks.

"The superintendent of prison of the concerned prison shall also get done the psychological evaluation of the appellant from the government medical hospital," the bench said, adding that a report of the evaluation be submitted to the court within eight weeks.
It posted the matter for hearing after 12 weeks.
On October 1, the apex court stayed the execution of the death penalty of Ahmed Bawa alias Abbu Abubakar Barelvi, one of the convicts in the case.

stories.headline: India-New Zealand FTA: Comm Min notifies tariff rate quota for apples, kiwifruit, Manuka honey
stories.title: India-New Zealand FTA: Comm Min notifies tariff rate quota for apples, kiwifruit, Manuka honey
stories.summary: India is allowing specified quantities of these products to enter at concessional import duty rates under the pact
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: With the India-New Zealand free trade agreement set to be effective on October 20, the Commerce Ministry on Monday laid out a procedure to allocate concessional duty-based quotas for imports of apples, kiwifruit, and Manuka honey from the island nation.

Under the pact, India is providing Tariff Rate Quotas (TRQs) in a calibrated manner for apples, kiwifruit, Manuka Honey and Albumins, along with Minimum Import Price (MIP) provisions and other safeguard measures.
This approach ensures calibrated imports while protecting the domestic farmers' interests.
"The procedure for allocation of TRQ under the India- New Zealand Free Trade Agreement is notified," the Directorate General of Foreign Trade (DGFT) said in a public notice.
India is allowing specified quantities of these products to enter at concessional import duty rates under the pact.
According to the notice, these provisions will take effect on October 20, 2026.
For apples, there will be no quota in the first year.
The quota will be 35,000 tonnes in the second year, rising to 37,500 tonnes in the third, 40,000 tonnes in the fourth and 42,500 tonnes in the fifth.
From the sixth year onwards, it will be 45,000 tonnes a year.
These imports will attract a 25 per cent duty, provided their cost, insurance and freight (CIF) value is at least USD 1.25 per kg.
The annual import window will run from April 1 to August 31.
At present, India has a 50 per cent import duty on apples.
